warmup.q: A provisioned table has 40,000 WCU and uses about 6,000. Every payment also adds to one item, MERCH#M-0042#TOTAL, and on Black Friday that item gets 1,500 updates a second. What happens to those updates?
options: Nothing bad: 7,500 used of 40,000 provisioned is well within capacity
Adaptive capacity gives the item a partition of its own and lends it the table's 32,500 spare units
About 500 a second are throttled: one item lives in one partition, and a partition takes at most 1,000 write units a second
DynamoDB splits the item's partition until the load fits, within a few minutes
warmup.why: The table's capacity is a sum over partitions; the per-partition ceiling isn't. An item lives in exactly one partition, and a partition serves at most 1,000 WCU however much the table has. Adaptive capacity can isolate a hot item in a partition of its own, but that partition still tops out at 1,000. A split divides key ranges, and one key can't be divided: the 2022 paper says a partition receiving high traffic to a single item won't benefit from a split. So about 500 updates a second are throttled, with the reason TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded.

sections.h: What runs when you call PutItem
sections.html:
This case study shows the track's partitioning ideas run as a managed service. DynamoDB cuts a table into ranges of hash values that split as they grow, lesson 1's hash-range scheme. It rebalances by splitting, by size and by traffic, instead of moving fixed shards (lesson 3). A tier of routers finds each key in a map kept by a metadata service (lesson 3 again). It relieves hot spots by itself up to a hard ceiling (lesson 2), and its global secondary indexes lag (lesson 4). Each partition is a small single-leader group, the replication of the Replication track's first lesson. The Data models track called DynamoDB a hash map of small sorted maps and designed one table for payments. Neither looked at the machines, and you can't log into them: AWS runs the servers. So setting up DynamoDB means designing the table and choosing its capacity, and both choices only make sense once you know what runs underneath. The 2022 USENIX ATC paper by Elhemali and others describes it. Build it up.

Version 1 is one server holding the whole table. The Data models track's first lesson showed where that ends: one disk, one CPU, and an outage when it dies.

Version 2 cuts the table into partitions. DynamoDB hashes the partition key, and each partition owns a contiguous range of hash values, lesson 1's hash-range sharding, stored as a B-tree (the Storage engines track's B+tree lesson) on a storage node's SSD. One storage node holds replicas of many partitions, from many tables of many customers. Now every request must find its partition, so a fleet of request routers sits in front, lesson 3's routing tier. A router authenticates the request (it caches IAM results, so an IAM hiccup doesn't stall it), checks the table's throughput budget, hashes the key and looks the partition up in a partition map. At launch each router downloaded a table's whole map on first use, and a fleet of cold routers flooded the metadata store. The fix the paper describes is MemDS, an in-memory metadata service, with a small cache on each router that refreshes in the background.

Version 3 copies every partition three times, one replica in each of three availability zones (separate data centres in one AWS Region). The three form a replication group that runs Multi-Paxos, a consensus protocol in the same family as Raft (the Consensus track builds Raft): replicas agree on one leader and one order of writes by majority vote. One replica is elected leader and holds a lease, a time-limited right to lead, that it keeps renewing. Only the leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads. For a write, it appends a record to its write-ahead log (the append-only record of changes from the Storage engines track's write-ahead logging lesson), sends it to its two peers, and acknowledges once two of the three, itself included, have it on disk. An eventually consistent read may go to any replica, which is why it can miss a write that just finished. If the leader dies, a follower calls an election, and the winner waits for the old leader's lease to expire, a couple of seconds, before it takes writes.

Version 4 heals quickly. Rebuilding a lost replica means copying its B-tree, which takes minutes, so the leader first adds a log replica that stores only recent log records. It joins in seconds, and writes can again get two of three acknowledgements while the full replica is rebuilt.

A table is a set of key ranges. Each range is a three-replica Paxos group with a leader and its own ceiling, and a fleet of routers looks up which group owns each key. Splits, capacity, indexes and global tables below all hang off that picture. The stepper follows one write through it.

sections.h: Every partition has a ceiling, so partitions split
sections.html:
A partition serves at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, and holds about 10 GB. (From the Data models track's DynamoDB lesson: a write unit is one write a second of up to 1 KB; a read unit is one strongly consistent read a second of up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent ones.) Those three numbers are why partitions split. Lesson 3 set fixed shard counts against shards that split as they grow; DynamoDB is the second kind, and it has three reasons to split.

At creation, a provisioned table gets enough partitions for its throughput, and each gets an equal share. The paper's example: 3,200 WCU needs 4 partitions of 800. Raise the table to 3,600 and each share becomes 900. Raise it to 6,000 and four partitions can't carry that, so each splits in two: 8 partitions of 750. Lower it to 5,000 and you keep 8, at 625 each, because partitions only ever split. They never merge.

Data splits partitions too. When one nears 10 GB it splits in two, and in the original design its share of the table's throughput was divided between the halves. A table with 1,000 WCU and 15 GB had two partitions of 500, and a key range taking 800 writes a second was throttled while the other half idled. The paper calls this throughput dilution.

Traffic splits partitions as well. When a partition's consumed throughput stays high, DynamoDB splits it for consumption, at a point chosen from the keys it has seen used rather than the middle of the range, so the busy keys land on both sides. That takes minutes. Two patterns can't be helped, and the paper names both: one item that takes the traffic, and a key range written in order, such as one partition key with a timestamp sort key, where every new write lands at the same end however you cut.

When a request needs more than its partition or table may give, DynamoDB throttles it: it refuses the request with HTTP 400 and changes nothing. The AWS SDK retries throttled requests with exponential backoff, so you first see higher latency, then an exception. The exception carries ThrottlingReasons naming the limit. TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded is a hot partition. TableWriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded is the table's provisioned capacity. An Index... reason is a GSI (section 4). More provisioned capacity fixes the second, and does nothing for the first.

DynamoDB Local does none of this. It's a single Java process for development. The docs say it ignores provisioned throughput, and it has no partitions, so it never splits and never throttles. The Try-it proves it. Test your throttling behaviour against the lab's model, or a real table.

try.title: Overload a 1 WCU table in Local, then read a real throttle
steps: With DynamoDB Local still running, read LocalNeverThrottlesDemo.kt. It provisions a table with one write unit a second, turns off the SDK's retries, and sends 1,000 writes from eight threads. Predict how many are throttled.
Then read the second block, from the AWS docs. That's what a throttle looks like on real DynamoDB; Local can't produce one.

Real DynamoDB would admit about one a second plus a few hundred saved-up burst units, and * throttle the rest. DynamoDB Local is one process with no partitions and no admission control. */ fun main() { val ddb = DynamoDbClient.builder() .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000")) .region(Region.US_EAST_1) .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz"))) // no SDK retries: a throttle would reach this code instead of being retried quietly .overrideConfiguration { it.retryStrategy(AwsRetryStrategy.doNotRetry()) } .build() val table = "one-wcu" if (table in ddb.listTables().tableNames()) ddb.deleteTable { it.tableName(table) } // provisioned mode: 1 read unit and 1 write unit a second for the whole table ddb.createTable { it.tableName(table) .attributeDefinitions(AttributeDefinition.builder().attributeName("pk").attributeType(ScalarAttributeType.S).build()) .keySchema(KeySchemaElement.builder().attributeName("pk").keyType(KeyType.HASH).build()) .billingMode(BillingMode.PROVISIONED) .provisionedThroughput { p -> p.readCapacityUnits(1).writeCapacityUnits(1) } } val provisioned = ddb.describeTable { it.tableName(table) }.table().provisionedThroughput() println("provisioned: ${provisioned.readCapacityUnits()} RCU, ${provisioned.writeCapacityUnits()} WCU") val consumed = DoubleAdder() val throttled = AtomicInteger() val started = System.nanoTime() val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) for (i in 0 until 1_000) pool.execute { try { val r = ddb.putItem { it.tableName(table) .item(mapOf( "pk" to AttributeValue.fromS("PAY#pay-%06d".format(i)), "amountMinor" to AttributeValue.fromN((500 + i * 7919 % 9501).toString()), )) .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL) } consumed.add(r.consumedCapacity().capacityUnits()) } catch (e: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException) { throttled.incrementAndGet() // what real DynamoDB sends when a table or a partition is out of tokens } } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES) val seconds = (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1e9 println("wrote 1,000 items in %.1f s, about %,d a second".format(seconds, (1_000 / seconds).toLong())) println("write units consumed: %,.1f".format(consumed.sum())) println("throttled: $throttled") ddb.deleteTable { it.tableName(table) } ddb.close() }

            "resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/CustomerOrders/index/OrderDateIndex"

}

sections.h: Capacity: provisioned with burst and adaptive capacity, or on-demand
sections.html:
Capacity is the number of read and write units DynamoDB admits for a table each second. You choose one of two modes, and the history of the first explains how both behave today.

In provisioned mode you set RCU and WCU and pay for them by the hour, used or not. The 2012 design enforced each partition's share at the partition with a token bucket: a counter refilled at the share's rate, which each request pays from. The AWS docs' example shows the flaw. 400 WCU over 4 partitions gives each 100. Send partition 4 150 writes a second and the others 50, and partition 4 is throttled 50 a second while the table uses 300 of its 400.

Burst capacity came first. A partition saves up to 300 seconds of its unused share and spends it on spikes. A partition that ran at 50 of its 100 for five minutes saved 15,000 units, enough for 150 a second for another 300 seconds. Then it throttles again. Burst covers spikes, not a partition that's always busy.

Adaptive capacity came next. Lesson 2 spread a hot key by hand; this is DynamoDB doing part of that job for you. When a partition is throttled while the table has unused units, DynamoDB raises that partition's share, as long as the table stays within its provisioned total and the partition within 1,000 WCU. Partition 4 gets its 150, because 50 + 50 + 50 + 150 = 300 fits in 400. The paper says this removed over 99.99% of the throttling from skewed access. It can also move a very busy item into a partition of its own, so that item gets the full 1,000 WCU.

Today's design is global admission control. A central service tracks the table's budget as tokens. Each request router keeps a local token bucket and refills it from that service every few seconds. Partitions keep buckets of their own as a second line of defence, capped so no table can take over a storage node. So a hot partition can use the table's spare units at once, and one key above 1,000 WCU is still throttled: the partition ceiling never moves.

In on-demand mode you set nothing and pay per request. A new on-demand table takes up to 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second. After that, DynamoDB admits up to double your previous peak at once and splits partitions ahead of the next peak. Beyond double it adds capacity as traffic grows, but the docs warn you can be throttled if you pass double your previous peak within 30 minutes. A per-table quota caps it, 40,000 units of each by default, and you can set your own lower maximum as a guard against a runaway bill. For a known launch you can pre-warm the table by raising its warm throughput.

Choose on-demand for new tables, for spiky traffic and for anything you can't forecast, such as a payments API whose evening peak is ten times its night. Choose provisioned, with auto scaling, for steady load that you can forecast and that runs most of the day: per unit it costs less. You can switch a table from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in 24 hours, and back at any time.

sections.h: Work that happens after the partition: GSIs, streams, TTL, backups, global tables
sections.html:
Several features copy each write somewhere else, after the partition has acknowledged it. Knowing that they're asynchronous explains how each one behaves.

A global secondary index is lesson 4's global index: a second table, partitioned by the indexed attribute, with partitions of its own. After a write commits, DynamoDB sends the change on to the index's partitions. The Data models track showed the result: an index can lag, so it answers only eventually consistent reads. It didn't show back-pressure. If an index can't keep up, because its provisioned write capacity is too low or its key is hot (merchantId with M-0042, or status with three values), DynamoDB throttles writes to the base table, and the exception names the index: IndexWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded. Give each GSI at least the base table's write capacity, and choose its key as carefully as the table's. Every index that holds an item costs a write when the item changes, which the Try-it counts.

DynamoDB Streams is the table's change log. Each insert, update or delete becomes a record, kept 24 hours, appearing exactly once, in order for each item (not across items). Each open shard belongs to one partition, so the stream grows shards as the table splits. Use it to feed Kafka or a reporting store; as the Data models track warned, a transaction's writes arrive as separate records.

TTL deletes items whose expiry attribute, a Number of epoch seconds, has passed, typically within a few days, without charging write units. Until then the expired item is still there, so reads must filter it out. The deletes reach the stream marked as service deletions, so a consumer can tell them from yours.

Point-in-time recovery keeps continuous backups for 1 to 35 days (35 by default) at one-second granularity. A restore builds a new table from partition snapshots plus the write-ahead logs DynamoDB archives to S3, and never touches the live table. It's the answer to a bad deploy that deleted payments.

Global tables copy a table to other Regions, and the Replication track's lesson on many leaders took them apart: MREC accepts writes in every Region and settles conflicts by last writer wins, and MRSC (generally available since June 2025) replicates each write to at least one other Region before it returns, across exactly three Regions. Underneath, each Region's replica is an ordinary table, with its own partitions, routers and ceilings from this lesson, so a hot key is just as hot in every Region.

      AttributeName=paymentId,AttributeType=S AttributeName=merchantId,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=status,AttributeType=S AttributeName=createdAt,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=sk,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --on-demand-throughput MaxReadRequestUnits=24000,MaxWriteRequestUnits=8000 \
  --warm-throughput ReadUnitsPerSecond=24000,WriteUnitsPerSecond=8000 \
  --global-secondary-indexes file://payments-gsis.json \
  --stream-specification StreamEnabled=true,StreamViewType=NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES \
  --deletion-protection-enabled
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name payments \
  --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt
aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name payments \
  --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true,RecoveryPeriodInDays=35

The key schema is the Data models track's design: pk spreads accounts over partitions, sk orders an account's items. Only key attributes are declared; every other attribute is up to each item. PAY_PER_REQUEST is on-demand, right for a payments API whose Black Friday is many times its night. The on-demand maximum caps the table at 8,000 writes a second, so a runaway retry loop gets throttled instead of billed; leave room above the real peak. Warm throughput lets a new table take the expected launch peak at once instead of growing into it; AWS charges for raising it, and it can't be lowered. The file holds the two GSIs, byPayment and byMerchant, with the multi-attribute sort key from the single-table lesson; each costs a write per item it holds. The stream with old and new images feeds the outbox to Kafka. Deletion protection makes delete-table fail until someone turns it off. TTL and point-in-time recovery need calls of their own.

The same table in Terraform, the way most teams keep it:

resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "payments" {
  name                        = "payments"
  billing_mode                = "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  hash_key                    = "pk"
  range_key                   = "sk"
  stream_enabled              = true
  stream_view_type            = "NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES"
  deletion_protection_enabled = true

  attribute {
    name = "pk"
    type = "S"
  }
  # ...one attribute block each for sk, paymentId, merchantId, status, createdAt

  on_demand_throughput {
    max_read_request_units  = 24000
    max_write_request_units = 8000
  }
  global_secondary_index {
    name            = "byPayment"
    projection_type = "ALL"
    key_schema {
      attribute_name = "paymentId"
      key_type       = "HASH"
    }
    key_schema {
      attribute_name = "sk"
      key_type       = "RANGE"
    }
  }
  # ...byMerchant: merchantId HASH, then status and createdAt RANGE
  ttl {
    attribute_name = "expiresAt"
    enabled        = true
  }
  point_in_time_recovery {
    enabled                 = true
    recovery_period_in_days = 35
  }
}

For steady load, provisioned is the other shape: --provisioned-throughput on the table and on each GSI, auto scaling registered through Application Auto Scaling, and every GSI's write capacity at least the table's. Before production, also check the key against your peak per key (no item or partition key above 1,000 WCU), turn on CloudWatch Contributor Insights to see the busiest and most throttled keys, and alarm on the throttle metrics, split by reason.

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: service quotas

analogy: Think of a bank with thousands of numbered safe-deposit vaults. You never go to a vault yourself: you hand your slip to any clerk at the front desk (a request router), who checks your ID, looks up which vault holds your box in a ledger of vault ranges (the partition map) and sends a runner. Each vault has three keyholders in three different buildings, and one of them, the head keyholder, must sign every change, with one other keyholder countersigning before you get a receipt. A vault has a fixed door: only so many visits a minute, however empty the rest of the bank is. When a vault gets too full or too busy, the bank splits its boxes into two new vaults overnight. The analogy breaks at the busiest single box: a real bank would let a crowd queue at one box, while DynamoDB turns the excess away at once with a throttle, and no split can help, because one box can't be in two vaults.
world: Your Quarkus payment service talks to DynamoDB through the AWS SDK, so a throttle first shows up as latency (the SDK retries with backoff) and only then as a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException or ThrottlingException. Log the throttling reason, not just the class: a key-range reason means a key design problem, and raising capacity won't fix it. Temporal activity retries on top of SDK retries multiply load on a hot partition, so cap them. The stream with old and new images is your outbox into Kafka; partition the Kafka topic by the same account key so per-item order survives. A nightly settlement batch that writes in sort-key order (all of one merchant, then the next) is the sequential pattern that splits can't help: shuffle the order, or spread the writes over many partition keys at once, and rate-limit to stay under 1,000 WCU per key range.
mistake: The most common mistake is treating the table's capacity as one pool: "we provisioned 40,000 WCU and use 6,000, so we can't be throttled." Teams then raise capacity when throttles appear, see no improvement, and raise it again. The table total is a sum of partition ceilings, and one partition key, or one GSI key such as status, can't exceed 1,000 WCU or 3,000 RCU. People make the mistake because the console shows table-level numbers and DynamoDB hides partitions entirely, and because DynamoDB Local never throttles, so nothing in development warns them. The fix: read the ThrottlingReasons (a KeyRange reason is a hot key, not a capacity shortfall), find the key with Contributor Insights, and spread it, either with a better key or with lesson 2's write sharding for counters and hot merchants.

b.title: DynamoDB (this lesson)
b.html:
route a request   request routers, run by AWS
the map           partition metadata in MemDS
unit of data      partition: a hash range, about 10 GB,
                  3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU
replication       three replicas in three AZs: Multi-Paxos
                  leader, write acked by 2 of 3
split             by size, by throughput, for consumption
move              DynamoDB places replicas by load
hot single key    one partition: 1,000 WCU, then throttled
you choose        key design, capacity mode, indexes

compare.note: The machinery is the same shape: a router that looks keys up in a map kept in replicated metadata, ranges of keys as the unit of placement, and a consensus group per range that orders writes. The difference is who runs it and what you're allowed to touch. In MongoDB you run every box, so you size the oplog, place the members and choose when the balancer works; the shard key is the one decision that's expensive to undo. In DynamoDB you touch only the key and the capacity, and in exchange you get hard per-partition ceilings that no setting can raise. A hot key fails the same way in both: one key can't be split, so its writes stay on one machine's leader.

hints: Round up with Longs: (a + b - 1) / b. bytes is a Long, and rcu and wcu fit in one once you call toLong().
Demand per partition: val demand = IntArray(partitions); for ((pk, units) in writes) demand[partitionOf(pk, partitions)] += units.
minOf takes three arguments: minOf(demand[p], share, PARTITION_MAX_WCU). Adaptive and burst extras are minOf(what's still wanted, room under the partition max, what's available).

drill.title: The table, its settings and its ceilings, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the AWS CLI calls that create an on-demand payments table with pk/sk, a NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES stream and deletion protection, then turn on TTL on expiresAt and point-in-time recovery. Then one line each: a partition's three ceilings, what a new on-demand table admits and how that grows, and why one hot item is throttled whatever the table's capacity.

answer.html: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name payments \ --attribute-definitions AttributeName=pk,AttributeType=S AttributeName=sk,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema AttributeName=pk,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=sk,KeyType=RANGE \ --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \ --stream-specification StreamEnabled=true,StreamViewType=NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES \ --deletion-protection-enabled aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name payments \ --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name payments \ --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true # a partition: 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU, about 10 GB; past those it splits (or throttles) # on-demand: 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second when new, then double the # previous peak at once; beyond double within 30 minutes may throttle # one hot item: one key lives in one partition, and no split can divide a key, # so it gets 1,000 WCU at most

recap: A request goes to any request router, which authenticates it, checks admission tokens, hashes the partition key and finds the partition in a map cached from MemDS.

Each partition is three replicas in three availability zones running Multi-Paxos. The leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads and acknowledges once 2 of 3 have the log record; eventually consistent reads may come from any replica.

A partition takes at most 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU and about 10 GB. Partitions split by size, by provisioned throughput and for consumption, never merge, and can't split one hot item or an in-order key range.

Throttling refuses a request with HTTP 400; ThrottlingReasons names the limit. Provisioned capacity gained burst (300 s of savings), adaptive capacity (spare table units to a hot partition) and global admission control; on-demand admits double the previous peak and starts at 4,000 writes a second.

GSIs, streams, TTL, PITR and global tables work after the partition commits: a GSI is a global index that lags and can back-pressure the table, streams order records per item for 24 hours, and global tables (the Replication track) run these same partitions in every Region.
DynamoDB Local is one process: it accepts every setting but models no partitions, splits, throttling or PITR.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "We're on on-demand now, so we can't be throttled. Throttling is a provisioned-mode problem." Explain what a partition is, which limits still apply in on-demand mode, and what you'd check when throttles appear.
explain.answer: DynamoDB cuts every table into partitions, each a range of partition key hashes held by three replicas in three availability zones, with a leader that takes the writes. Every partition has fixed ceilings in both modes: 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second and about 10 GB. On-demand removes the number we used to set, but it doesn't remove those ceilings, and it adds two table-level limits of its own: it admits up to double the previous peak at once (and may throttle if we pass double within 30 minutes), and there's a per-table quota, 40,000 units by default, plus any maximum we configure. So a single hot item, such as a merchant's running total at 1,500 writes a second, is throttled in on-demand exactly as in provisioned, because one key lives in one partition and no split can divide it. A GSI with a skewed key throttles our base-table writes too. When throttles appear I'd read the ThrottlingReasons: KeyRange means a hot key or range, so we fix the key or shard it; MaxOnDemandThroughput or AccountLimit means a limit we can raise; for a launch I'd pre-warm the table. Then I'd turn on Contributor Insights to find the keys.

deeper.html:
The paper spends as much time on correctness as on speed. The core replication protocol is specified in TLA+ and model checked, and new features that touch it are added to the specification first. Every log record and message carries a checksum; logs are archived to S3 with a manifest, and the archiver checks every entry belongs to the right table and partition and that sequence numbers have no holes. A background scrub compares the three live replicas with each other and with a replica rebuilt offline from the archived logs, to catch bit rot that nothing else would.

Backups use the same logs. On-demand backups and point-in-time restore are built from the write-ahead logs archived in S3 plus periodic partition snapshots, so taking a backup costs the live table nothing. A restore picks the nearest snapshot before the requested second for every partition, replays the logs up to that second, and writes a new table.

Failure detection has a subtle problem the paper calls gray failure (the Faults, time and truth track returns to it): a follower may lose contact with the leader while the leader is fine and serving everyone else. If that follower called an election, it would interrupt a healthy partition, and the new leader would wait out the old lease. So a follower that wants to call an election first asks the other replicas whether they can see the leader, and backs off if they can. That one change cut spurious elections sharply.

The metadata story is a lesson in caches. Routers that cache a whole table's map work at a hit rate of about 99.75%, but a fleet of cold routers sends every request to the metadata store at once. MemDS answers every lookup, and each router's cache refreshes asynchronously on every hit, so MemDS sees the same load whether caches are warm or cold. If a router's map is stale, the storage node it reached answers with the new membership or an error that sends the router back to MemDS: the same idea as MongoDB's StaleConfig in lesson 7.
